newsitem.title: USA: Copper hits five-week high on supply worries.
newsitem.headline: Copper hits five-week high on supply worries.

text.p: Copper prices reached a five-week high Thursday ahead of a report Friday that is expected to confirm that global supplies are dwindling.

Heating oil prices fell sharply in New York for the second straight day following a similar drop in London. Cocoa reached a six-week high on robust world demand and soybeans tumbled on bearish export news.
In copper, strong seasonal demand has shrunk warehouse supplies in London and the U.S. and traders said demand is increasing.
"There's been a good underlying tone for some weeks and we're coming into what is seasonally a good demand period," said Fred Demler, a trader with E.D.&F. Man.
Demler said a London Metal Exchange storage report Friday may show another large drawdown of supplies.
Copper stocks in COMEX approved warehouses fell 584 tons Wednesday to 18,242 tons, following a 8,626 metric ton drawdown in LME stocks Tuesday to 220,950 metric tons.
COMEX December copper closed up 1.90 cents at 92.25 cents a lb.
Heating oil prices plunged Thursday at the New York Mercantile Exchange in reaction to a similar drop in gas oil futures in London and to an industry report showing greater-than-expected supplies.
"Gas oil in London just got pummeled, which sent shudders through heating oil, and the rest of the oil complex naturally reacted," said Bob Yawger, a trader with E. D. & F. Man International Inc.
Gas oil is the European equivalent of heating oil.
Also, the bearish American Petroleum Institute report late Tuesday continued to weigh on heating oil. The report showed a larger-than-expected build in distillate inventories, including heating oil.
NYMEX heating oil for November delivery plummeted 3.05 cents a gallon to 70.92 cents. The price of heating oil has risen more than 30 percent in the last three months on historically low supplies.
November crude oil settled 81 cents lower at $24.26 a barrel and November gasoline fell 2.07 cents at 63.52 cents a gallon.
Cocoa futures at New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange jumped, bolstered by continued optimism over surprisingly strong third-quarter use.

Traders said the unexpected increase in third-quarter German grindings reported Wednesday, tacked on to a sharp upturn last week on both U.K. and Dutch grindings, reignited speculative buying. The next key indicator of consumer demand is due in a week, when the U.S. third-quarter grindings are released.
CSCE December cocoa futures rose $17 to $1,402 a metric ton. Wednesday's rise, which dealers said was fuelled by speculative and industry buying, marked cocoa's fifth straight positive close.
Soybean futures at the Chicago Board of Trade tumbled in reaction to bearish government export sales data released early Thursday.
"People were disappointed in the bean sales. They were talking yesterday of maybe over one million tons but it didn't get there," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co.

The Agriculture Department early Thursday said U.S. soybean net export sales during the week ended October 3 were 582,400 metric tons. Even the 55,000 metric tons that it reported was sold to China was disappointing, traders expected a much larger amount.
CBOT November soybeans closed November down eight cents at $7.30-1/4 per bushel.
